lead: A seismic transducer measures vibration with a proof mass hung on a spring and damper inside a case. When the case moves, the mass lags behind. The relative motion between mass and case is the output. Below the natural frequency this motion follows acceleration; above it, it follows displacement. The same second-order model therefore explains two instruments: the accelerometer and the seismometer. Accelerometers fire airbags, watch machine bearings and level phones. Seismometers record earthquakes. This chapter derives the mass-spring-damper response, shows how to choose the working range, and connects it to piezoelectric and capacitive sensing.
prereq: You need the second-order dynamic characteristics of sensors (natural frequency, damping ratio, amplitude ratio) and piezoelectric transducers for the sensing element.

sections.h3: A mass on a spring and damper

blocks.text: Fix a case to a vibrating surface. Inside, a seismic mass m sits on a spring of stiffness k and a damper of coefficient c. Let x(t) be the mass displacement and y(t) the case displacement, both measured in metres from rest. The relative displacement is z = x − y. This z is what most seismic sensors actually measure.

blocks.where: m is the seismic mass in kg; c is the damping coefficient in N·s/m; k is the spring constant in N/m; z is the relative displacement in m; y is the case displacement in m; t is time in s.

blocks.text: Divide by m and write the standard second-order form. The natural angular frequency is ω<sub>n</sub> = √(k/m) rad/s, and the natural frequency is f<sub>n</sub> = (1/2π)√(k/m) Hz. The damping ratio is ζ = c/(2√(km)). For a sinusoidal case motion y = Y sin(2πft), define the frequency ratio r = f/f<sub>n</sub>, where f is the vibration frequency in Hz.

blocks.where: H = Z ω<sub>n</sub>² / A is the normalised amplitude ratio: the relative displacement Z per unit case acceleration A, multiplied by ω<sub>n</sub>² so that H = 1 at low frequency; D = √((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²) is the denominator, so H = 1/D; r = f/f<sub>n</sub> is dimensionless; ζ is the damping ratio.

blocks.text: The relative displacement amplitude is Z = (A/ω<sub>n</sub>²) H, where A is the case acceleration amplitude in m/s². At low r, H ≈ 1, so Z ∝ A: the output reads acceleration. At high r, the displacement ratio Z/Y = r²H tends to 1, so the output reads displacement. The phase lag is φ = arctan(2ζr/(1 − r²)), with a 90° lag at r = 1.

An accelerometer is a seismic transducer used with f ≪ f<sub>n</sub>, usually r below about 0.2 to 0.4 (with ζ = 0.7, H stays within 1 % of 1 up to r ≈ 0.4). Then H is close to 1 and the relative displacement is almost exactly A/ω<sub>n</sub>². The sensor output is proportional to acceleration. A high f<sub>n</sub> gives a wide usable band. A small mass and a stiff spring raise f<sub>n</sub>.

items: Piezoelectric accelerometer: a crystal or ceramic stack is compressed by the seismic mass. It produces charge q = d·F, where d is the piezoelectric charge constant in C/N and F is the dynamic force in N. A charge amplifier converts q to a voltage. It cannot measure true DC acceleration.
Capacitive MEMS accelerometer: a silicon proof mass moves between capacitor plates, and the capacitance change gives acceleration. It can measure DC and is small enough for phones and airbags.

blocks.text: Damping is chosen near ζ = 0.6 to 0.7. Damping near ζ = 0.7 removes the peak near r = 1 and extends the flat band to higher r, and it keeps the phase shift close to linear, so the waveform stays faithful. Too little damping gives a sharp peak at r = 1; too much damping slows the response.

Mounting matters. The case, adhesive or magnet has its own resonance. If that mounting resonance falls near the measurement band, the output shows a false peak. Keep the mounting resonance well above the highest frequency you need. The same rule applies to the sensor's own resonance: never use an accelerometer at or near f<sub>n</sub>.

A seismometer uses the other end of the curve. With f ≫ f<sub>n</sub>, the mass hardly follows the case, so the relative displacement z approaches the case displacement y. The instrument then reads ground displacement. A low f<sub>n</sub> needs a soft spring and a large mass. A short-period seismometer has a higher f<sub>n</sub>; a long-period one has a lower f<sub>n</sub>. Damping near critical reduces the free ringing after a shock.

In a car airbag, a MEMS accelerometer detects the sudden deceleration of a crash and the electronic control unit fires the bag within milliseconds. In machine condition monitoring, an accelerometer bolted to a bearing housing picks up vibration; a growing peak at a bearing frequency warns of wear. In earthquake sensing, a network of seismometers records arrival times and amplitudes. For strong local motion, an accelerometer is preferred because it does not clip as easily as a soft seismometer. In medicine, small body-worn accelerometers count steps and grade activity, measure tremor and gait in rehabilitation, and an activity sensor inside a rate-responsive pacemaker raises the pacing rate when the patient moves.

figure.caption: The amplitude ratio H against r = f/f<sub>n</sub>. With ζ = 0.7 the curve stays within 1 % of 1 up to r ≈ 0.4, the accelerometer band; both worked examples sit inside it. With ζ = 0.1 the peak at resonance reaches 5.0.

examples.question: An accelerometer has natural frequency f<sub>n</sub> = 10 kHz and damping ratio ζ = 0.7. Find the amplitude ratio H and the percentage error at a vibration frequency f = 1 kHz.
steps: Error: (H − 1) × 100% = 0.015%. Positive means the reading is high.
examples.answer: At 1 kHz the amplitude ratio is H = 1.00015, so the accelerometer reads 0.015 % high.
examples.check:
import math
fn = 10000.0
f = 1000.0
zeta = 0.7
r = f / fn
H = 1 / math.sqrt((1 - r*r)**2 + (2*zeta*r)**2)
err = (H - 1) * 100
print(round(H, 5))
print(round(err, 3))

examples.question: A piezoelectric accelerometer has a seismic mass of 10 g on a mounting stiffness of 4 × 10⁶ N/m. (a) Find its natural frequency. (b) Find the damping coefficient for ζ = 0.7. (c) Find the relative displacement for a steady 1 g (9.81 m/s²). (d) Find H, the amplitude error and the phase lag for a 1 kHz vibration, and the relative displacement for a 5 g amplitude at that frequency.
steps: (c) Z = A/ω<sub>n</sub>² = 9.81 / (2.0 × 10⁴)² = 9.81 / 4 × 10⁸ = 2.45 × 10⁻⁸ m = 24.5 nm per g. The movement is tiny, so the sensing element must be very stiff and sensitive.
examples.answer: f<sub>n</sub> = 3183 Hz, c = 280 N·s/m, 24.5 nm per g; at 1 kHz H = 0.9971 (0.29 % low) with a 26.0° lag, and 5 g gives 0.122 µm.
examples.check:
import math
m = 0.01
k = 4e6
z = 0.7
wn = math.sqrt(k/m)
fn = wn/2/math.pi
c = 2*z*math.sqrt(k*m)
r = 1000/fn
H = 1/math.sqrt((1-r*r)**2+(2*z*r)**2)
print(round(fn), round(c), 9.81/wn**2, round(H, 4), round(math.degrees(math.atan2(2*z*r, 1-r*r)), 1), 5*9.81/wn**2*H)

traps: Using an accelerometer at or near its natural frequency: H becomes large and the phase shifts, so the waveform is wrong even if the sensor does not break.
Forgetting the mounting resonance: a stud, glue or magnet can add a peak inside the measurement band.
Mixing the two ratios: H = 1/D is the acceleration response; Z/Y = r²/D is the displacement response used by a seismometer.
Dropping units in f<sub>n</sub> = (1/2π)√(k/m): use k in N/m and m in kg to get Hz; grams or N/mm give a wrong frequency.
Thinking zero damping is best: low ζ gives a sharp resonance peak and a large phase change; about ζ = 0.7 is often chosen.

quiz.q: Define the natural frequency and damping ratio of the seismic mass.
quiz.a: f<sub>n</sub> = (1/2π)√(k/m), where k is spring constant in N/m and m is seismic mass in kg. ζ = c/(2√(km)), where c is damping coefficient in N·s/m.

quiz.q: Why is an accelerometer used with f ≪ f<sub>n</sub>?
quiz.a: Then r is small, H ≈ 1, and relative displacement is proportional to acceleration; the scale factor is nearly constant and phase shift is small.

quiz.q: A seismometer has f<sub>n</sub> = 1 Hz and ζ = 0.7. Find Z/Y at f = 10 Hz.
An accelerometer with f<sub>n</sub> = 10 kHz is mounted with a bracket whose resonance is 6 kHz. The machine vibrates at 5 kHz. Explain the risk.
quiz.a: The bracket resonance lies in or near the measurement band. It amplifies 5 kHz motion and adds phase shift; the reading is not the true machine vibration. Move the mounting resonance higher or filter below it.

quiz.q: Why is ζ around 0.6–0.7 used in accelerometers?
quiz.a: It removes the peak near r = 1 and extends the flat band to higher r, and it keeps the phase shift close to linear, so the waveform stays faithful. Too little damping gives a sharp peak at r = 1; too much damping slows the response.

quiz.q: Why can a piezoelectric accelerometer not measure a constant acceleration?
quiz.a: A constant acceleration gives a constant force and constant charge. The charge leaks away through the amplifier and insulation, so the output falls to zero; it responds only to changing acceleration.

beyond: Not for the exam. Most accelerometers today are MEMS devices with capacitive or piezoresistive sensing and the signal conditioning on one chip. Earthquake networks combine seismometers with accelerometers and GPS, and vibration data feed predictive maintenance. Search: MEMS accelerometer, strong-motion accelerograph.
